variants.title: Cross the four boundaries
variants.context: Defense in depth gives each stage a different failure: the context boundary runs before inference, the capability boundary constrains tools during inference, the decision boundary checks the consequence before it happens, and the response boundary records, monitors, and reduces exposure afterwards.
variants.prompt: A support assistant answers a question and then proposes a refund. Put the boundaries in order.

items.text: Validate the structured output, recheck policy, and require approval before the refund is committed.
Expose only the tools and scopes this request needs, bound to the caller's current authorization.
Authenticate the caller, minimize the data, and label retrieved content as untrusted before inference.
Log the versioned decision, monitor interventions, and reduce exposure if incidents follow.

variants.hint: Which check happens before the model sees anything?
variants.explanation: Each boundary owns a different failure, so the consequence is checked separately from the text the model produced.

variants.title: Cross the four boundaries
variants.context: Defense in depth gives each stage a different failure: the context boundary runs before inference, the capability boundary constrains tools during inference, the decision boundary checks the consequence before it happens, and the response boundary records, monitors, and reduces exposure afterwards.
variants.prompt: A retrieved wiki page contains hidden instructions telling the agent to export customer records. Put the defenses in order.

items.text: The proposed tool argument is validated against policy, and the export is refused before it runs.
The refusal, the source identifier, and the policy version are recorded and the pattern is monitored.
The request is issued a tool set with no export scope, tied to this caller's permissions.
The retrieved page is labeled as untrusted content and kept separate from the system instructions.

variants.hint: Which boundary would still hold if the model followed the injected instruction?
variants.explanation: The model may be fooled, so least privilege and deterministic validation are what keep the injection from becoming a consequence.

variants.title: Cross the four boundaries
variants.context: Defense in depth gives each stage a different failure: the context boundary runs before inference, the capability boundary constrains tools during inference, the decision boundary checks the consequence before it happens, and the response boundary records, monitors, and reduces exposure afterwards.
variants.prompt: A tenant asks a question whose answer would require another tenant's invoice. Put the controls in order.

items.text: The decision, the retrieved source identifiers, and the tenant scope are stored for review.
Data tools are bound to the tenant scope rather than to a shared service credential.
The drafted answer is inspected for sensitive data before it is returned to the caller.
The caller's tenant scope is resolved and only that tenant's documents are retrieved.

variants.hint: Tenant isolation is enforced more than once on this path.
variants.explanation: An accurate model can still reveal the wrong tenant's data, so authorization is enforced at every data and tool boundary.

variants.title: Run the control plane
variants.context: Guardrails run as a versioned control plane in four steps: observe policy outcomes and queue health, contain by disabling capability or rolling back the bundle, investigate by replaying the versioned path, then improve with regression cases before exposure is earned again.
variants.prompt: Refusal rates on one language slice jump after a prompt change. Put the control plane response in order.

items.text: Add the cases as regressions, repair the control, and earn the exposure back.
Switch the affected path to answer only mode while the cause is unknown.
Replay the versioned path to identify the failed boundary and estimate affected users.
Notice the slice regression in policy outcomes, overrides, and user reports.

variants.hint: What happens between noticing and understanding?
variants.explanation: Containment comes before investigation, so users stop absorbing a regression while the replay is still running.

variants.title: Run the control plane
variants.context: Guardrails run as a versioned control plane in four steps: observe policy outcomes and queue health, contain by disabling capability or rolling back the bundle, investigate by replaying the versioned path, then improve with regression cases before exposure is earned again.
variants.prompt: An abuse wave saturates the human review queue during a product launch. Put the response in order.

items.text: Add the pattern to the evaluation set, repair the control, and rehearse the response.
Lower exposure by disabling the affected capability rather than letting the queue grow.
Replay the flagged traffic to separate the abuse pattern from ordinary launch volume.
Watch queue age, escalation volume, and tool denials climb past their thresholds.

variants.hint: Queue capacity is a release gate, not only an operations metric.
variants.explanation: An unserviceable queue is contained by reducing exposure, because a backlog of unreviewed cases is itself an unsafe state.

variants.title: Run the control plane
variants.context: Guardrails run as a versioned control plane in four steps: observe policy outcomes and queue health, contain by disabling capability or rolling back the bundle, investigate by replaying the versioned path, then improve with regression cases before exposure is earned again.
variants.prompt: A rollback restored the previous model but left the newer policy bundle in place. Put the response in order.

items.text: Replay affected requests to find which decisions were made under the mismatched pair.
Roll the policy bundle back to the version that matches the restored model.
Add a version pairing check to the release path and rehearse the rollback again.
Detect that decisions now cite a model and policy version pair that was never evaluated together.

variants.hint: Which artifacts have to move together?
variants.explanation: The model and its policy bundle are one evaluated pair, so a partial rollback creates a configuration that no evidence covers.

variants.title: Size the safety gate
variants.context: A safety triage gate has four cells. Unsafe cases times recall are the true positives, safe cases times the false positive rate are the safe requests interrupted, and their sum is the review queue that real reviewers have to work through.
variants.prompt: An assistant handles 20,000 requests, of which 500 are unsafe. The detector has 90 percent recall and a 2 percent false positive rate. How many cases reach the review queue?
variants.hint: The queue holds both kinds of flag.
variants.explanation: 450 true positives plus 2 percent of the 19,500 safe requests, which is 390, gives a queue of 840.

mistakes.feedback: That counts only the unsafe cases caught; interrupted safe requests are reviewed too.
That applies the 2 percent to all 20,000 requests instead of to the safe ones.

variants.title: Size the safety gate
variants.context: A safety triage gate has four cells. Unsafe cases times recall are the true positives, safe cases times the false positive rate are the safe requests interrupted, and their sum is the review queue that real reviewers have to work through.
variants.prompt: A high recall point runs over 10,000 requests with 400 unsafe cases, at 97 percent recall and an 8 percent false positive rate. Reviewers can handle 700 cases. How many queued cases exceed capacity?
variants.hint: Build the queue first, then compare it with the capacity.
variants.explanation: 388 true positives plus 768 interrupted safe requests make a queue of 1,156, which is 456 above the capacity of 700.

mistakes.feedback: That is the size of the queue, not the amount by which it exceeds capacity.
That treats all 400 unsafe cases as flagged; recall is 97 percent, so 388 are caught.

variants.title: Size the safety gate
variants.context: A safety triage gate has four cells. Unsafe cases times recall are the true positives, safe cases times the false positive rate are the safe requests interrupted, and their sum is the review queue that real reviewers have to work through.
variants.prompt: A release gate caps interruption of safe requests at 5 percent. Over 20,000 requests with 1,000 unsafe cases, the detector interrupts 760 safe requests. What is the false positive rate?
variants.hint: The rate is measured over the population it applies to.
variants.explanation: 760 interruptions over 19,000 safe requests is 4 percent, which passes the 5 percent interruption gate.

mistakes.feedback: That divides by all 20,000 requests instead of by the safe ones.
That divides by the 1,000 unsafe cases, which are not the population being interrupted.

variants.title: Fail closed on consequence
variants.context: The model proposes and deterministic application controls decide. A missing or uncertain control must never silently grant high impact authority, so consequential paths fail closed, tools stay narrow and identity bound, and irreversible actions need a fresh confirmation.
variants.prompt: The policy service times out while an agent is about to commit a high value write. What should the runtime do?
options: Commit the write and re-evaluate the policy when the service returns.
Commit the write if the last cached policy decision allowed a similar request.
Refuse the write and fall back to a non-actioning mode.
optionFeedback: Re-evaluating afterwards happens after the consequence already landed.
A cached decision about a different request is not a decision about this one.
An unavailable control cannot grant authority, so the consequential path fails closed.
variants.hint: What does a missing answer from a control mean for a consequential action?
variants.explanation: A missing or uncertain control never silently grants high impact authority, so the write is refused rather than assumed safe.

variants.title: Fail closed on consequence
variants.context: The model proposes and deterministic application controls decide. A missing or uncertain control must never silently grant high impact authority, so consequential paths fail closed, tools stay narrow and identity bound, and irreversible actions need a fresh confirmation.
variants.prompt: An agent needs to issue refunds. The team is choosing between a general database tool and a narrow refund draft tool. Which is safer and why?
options: The general tool, because a single audited surface is easier to monitor.
The general tool, because the policy layer validates every query anyway.
The narrow tool, because it limits what any unexpected output can do.
optionFeedback: One broad surface concentrates authority rather than constraining it.
Validating arbitrary queries is far harder than validating one structured action.
Narrow, identity bound tools shrink the blast radius of an unexpected model output.
variants.hint: Ask what the worst allowed call can do in each design.
variants.explanation: Excessive functionality is a design choice, so narrow tools bound to the caller's authorization are preferred over open ended access.

variants.title: Fail closed on consequence
variants.context: The model proposes and deterministic application controls decide. A missing or uncertain control must never silently grant high impact authority, so consequential paths fail closed, tools stay narrow and identity bound, and irreversible actions need a fresh confirmation.
variants.prompt: An assistant proposes sending a message to 40,000 customers, and the request was approved for a draft an hour ago. What should happen?
options: Send it, because the earlier approval already covers this workflow.
Send it and record a compensating action in case the content is wrong.
Require a fresh confirmation, because the action is irreversible and externally visible.
optionFeedback: An approval for a draft is not an approval to send it to customers.
Compensation cannot recall a message that recipients have already read.
Irreversible, externally visible actions need a confirmation tied to this action.
variants.hint: Which of these actions can actually be undone?
variants.explanation: Fresh confirmation is required for irreversible or externally visible actions, because reversibility is what decides how much authority a control can delegate.

variants.title: Fill the risk contract
variants.context: A risk contract connects a use case to an enforceable response. It names the affected party, the unsafe behavior, the system path the behavior travels, the severity and reversibility of one event, and the response the system takes.
variants.prompt: Match each field of the risk contract to what it records.

pairs.label: Affected party
pairs.detail: The user, a person described by the output, an operator, a tenant, or the public.

pairs.label: Unsafe behavior
pairs.detail: Disclosure, discriminatory treatment, harmful assistance, manipulation, or an unauthorized action.

pairs.label: System path
pairs.detail: Direct input, retrieved content, memory, model output, tool argument, or downstream side effect.

pairs.label: Severity and reversibility
pairs.detail: The impact of a single event and whether the system can undo it.

pairs.label: Response
pairs.detail: Allow, transform, refuse, request confirmation, route to review, or disable a capability.

variants.hint: One field decides how strong the response is allowed to be.
variants.explanation: A guardrail is designed from a specific party, behavior, path, and severity, not from a generic list of harmful words.

variants.title: Fill the risk contract
variants.context: A risk contract connects a use case to an enforceable response. It names the affected party, the unsafe behavior, the system path the behavior travels, the severity and reversibility of one event, and the response the system takes.
variants.prompt: A support assistant showed one tenant another tenant's invoice. Match each detail to its contract field.

pairs.label: Affected party
pairs.detail: The customer whose invoice was exposed, who never used the assistant.

pairs.label: Unsafe behavior
pairs.detail: Disclosure of another tenant's billing record in an otherwise accurate answer.

pairs.label: System path
pairs.detail: A retrieval call that ran under a shared service credential instead of the caller's scope.

pairs.label: Severity and reversibility
pairs.detail: High impact and not undoable, since the reader has already seen the record.

pairs.label: Response
pairs.detail: Refuse the answer, scope retrieval to the caller, and disable the shared credential path.

variants.hint: The affected party here is not the person who typed the question.
variants.explanation: Naming the party and the path is what turns a vague privacy concern into a control that can be enforced and tested.

variants.title: Fill the risk contract
variants.context: A risk contract connects a use case to an enforceable response. It names the affected party, the unsafe behavior, the system path the behavior travels, the severity and reversibility of one event, and the response the system takes.
variants.prompt: An agent drafted a large refund after reading a hostile document. Match each detail to its contract field.

pairs.label: Affected party
pairs.detail: The operator whose account and budget the refund would have moved.

pairs.label: Unsafe behavior
pairs.detail: An unauthorized tool action proposed from instructions the user never wrote.

pairs.label: System path
pairs.detail: Injected text inside retrieved content that reached the tool argument.

pairs.label: Severity and reversibility
pairs.detail: High impact, partially recoverable, since a committed transfer needs a manual reversal.

pairs.label: Response
pairs.detail: Require fresh confirmation, narrow the tool scope, and add the case to the evaluation set.

variants.hint: Follow the instruction from where it entered to where it would have acted.
variants.explanation: The system path names where to place the control, which is why an injection is contained at the tool boundary rather than in the prompt.
